video-electrical-upgrades-1tz47h-uusc-yo.title: Grounding a Two-Prong Outlet in an Unfinished Basement: GFCI Option and AFCI Laundry-Circuit Upgrade
video-electrical-upgrades-1tz47h-uusc-yo.summary: The video identifies an ungrounded two-prong outlet and explains how grounding works, then presents two remediation paths: installing a GFCI receptacle to provide protection without pulling a new ground, or running a dedicated equipment-grounding conductor (EGC) by replacing wiring. The team opts for upgrading the laundry circuit with 12‑gauge wire, a conduit-fed metal box on a concrete wall, and an AFCI protected breaker, followed by testing with a receptacle tester to verify ground status and correct polarity. The segment emphasizes safety, code considerations (12 AWG for laundry, AFCI protection), and verification steps before re-energizing the circuit.

video-electrical-upgrades-2i8bmttbzj8-yo.summary: This This Old House segment guides a homeowner through safely replacing an aged ceiling fixture in a house built in 1960. The hosts inspect the new LED fixture for pre-1985 wiring compatibility, demonstrate turning off power at the panel, and address the risks of using outdated cloth NM cable with low temperature ratings. To accommodate modern fixtures, they splice in new wiring and install a new metal junction box in the ceiling, routing conductors through an attic/crawl-space path, bonding the ground, and reassembling the fixture with LED bulbs. The episode emphasizes heat management near junction boxes, explains the 60°C versus 90°C insulation jacket ratings, and demonstrates how to identify cable types (NM, NM-B) and what labeling signifies for safe installation.

video-electrical-upgrades-4talvrw2n-u-yo.title: Post Light Replacement with LED Diode Fixture and Astronomical Timer
video-electrical-upgrades-4talvrw2n-u-yo.summary: This Old House guides a full exterior lighting upgrade centered on replacing a rotted lamp-post, upgrading the switch and wiring, and installing a modern, LED-based lighting ensemble. The video demonstrates removing the old post, pouring a quick-set post foundation, installing a new aluminum post with an LED diode fixture, routing wiring, replacing the wall switch with a weatherproof box and an astronomical time clock, and matching a wall sconce to the new post light for a cohesive exterior look. The sequence emphasizes safety (power shutoff), weatherproofing, and choosing long-lasting, low-maintenance lighting components.

video-electrical-upgrades-7wofufavbvs-yo.title: Two-Tool Electrical Projects: Lineman Pliers and a Flat-Head Screwdriver
video-electrical-upgrades-7wofufavbvs-yo.summary: This Old House’s Ask This Old House video foregrounds a minimalist approach to basic electrical tasks, arguing that two tools—the lineman pliers and a flat-head screwdriver—are sufficient for many common jobs. The segment demonstrates wire work (cutting, stripping, and twisting/splicing), accessing electrical boxes by removing covers, and removing knockouts. It also shows using a lock-nut push tool to remove knockouts and to drive staples, with a brief note on clearing obstructions (using a chisel when needed). The tone is practical and conversational, emphasizing tool economy and flexibility over a large tool kit.

video-electrical-upgrades-9756ycjrcss-yo.title: Install an Electrical Receptacle in a Kitchen Island: Box Location, Wiring, and AFCI/GFCI Testing
video-electrical-upgrades-9756ycjrcss-yo.summary: This Old House chronicles a kitchen-island upgrade to add a dedicated receptacle where none existed. Heath and Katie locate a feed that presumably serves the island, verify that power can be safely de-energized (using a non-contact tester and a meter), and then trace the wire with a toner to confirm its path toward a wall outlet location. They mark and cut a precise opening in the island’s cabinet/back panel, then install a new junction box and route BX/metal-clad cable through a protected bushing with a 90° connector. After wiring the receptacle (ground to green, neutral to silver, hot to brass) and securing the box, they install an AFCI-protected circuit (and test a GFCI function) to ensure protection for the new outlet. The finished test confirms the mixer and other devices work, and the homeowners can use the island for baking with confidence. Throughout, the video emphasizes safety steps (de-energize, confirm with a meter, proper notch and spacing, and appropriate connections) and documentation of the process from locating the feed to testing the finished circuit.

video-electrical-upgrades-awg-gqh1wfq-yo.title: Powering a Backyard Shed: trenching, conduit, and panel installation (Ask This Old House)
video-electrical-upgrades-awg-gqh1wfq-yo.summary: In this This Old House episode, Heath and Jeff plan, trench, and wire a new electrical feed from the house to a newly built shed. The team assesses the site, routes a trench between the shed and the house, installs outdoor conduit with LB and expansion fittings, and places a ground system. They set up a panel, pull feeders, and wire the shed to meet minimum code requirements (at least one receptacle and one light), then perform a power-on test to verify the install. The process emphasizes safe coordination (Dig Safe), trench backfill with a sand bed, protection of the conduit, proper conduit orientation to reduce water intrusion, and a reminder that live work should be performed by a licensed electrician when disconnecting service.

video-electrical-upgrades-bbuvfqwnfz4-yo.title: Upgrading a 3-Way Switch to a Smart 3-Way System (This Old House)
video-electrical-upgrades-bbuvfqwnfz4-yo.summary: This how-to video from This Old House teaches upgrading a traditional three-way lighting circuit to a smart three-way arrangement. It distinguishes single-pole versus three-way configurations, identifies the common vs travelers on a three-way switch, and walks through power-down safety, removal of existing switches, and wiring a smart master switch. The tutorial covers two approaches for the downstream box: using a remote add-on (or keeping the mechanical switch for guest use), wiring the master with ground and properly paired travelers, creating a feed/pigtail, and securely tucking conductors. It also demonstrates linking the master and add-on, and confirms two-location control by testing from both switch locations.

video-electrical-upgrades-bifohd2d04y-yo.title: Sub Panel Siting, Feeder Strategy, and Service Upgrade Considerations
video-electrical-upgrades-bifohd2d04y-yo.summary: This Old House discusses installing and configuring a sub panel to serve a distant wing of a house (office, master suite, and garage mechanical space) when the main panel is remote. The video covers siting the sub panel in the proposed area near an open sectional wall, pouring a concrete slab and adding a 2x4 wall to mount the panel, and routing a single feeder cable into the sub panel rather than running many circuits. It then explains the relationship to the main service (initial 100 A panel in the main house), the plan to upgrade to a newer panel with arc-fault and GFCI protection, and the consideration of increasing service capacity from 100 A to 200 A or potentially 400 A based on load calculations that include heating/cooling, cooking, lighting, and future EV charging. The utility’s requirement to justify a 400 A service is highlighted, along with the practical steps of performing load calculations and the need to “homework” the sizing before upgrading.

video-electrical-upgrades-c8i2pqhmx-u-yo.title: How to Install an Electric Lantern | Copper Lantern Fabrication, Finishing, and Exterior Installation (New Orleans)
video-electrical-upgrades-c8i2pqhmx-u-yo.summary: This Old House follows a New Orleans artisan and the project homeowner as they craft and install a New Orleans–style electric lantern. The episode covers: (1) the Bourbon Street lantern design tradition and what makes it distinctly New Orleans; (2) copper fabrication from raw copper sheets using a foot shear, a notcher, and hand snips to form decorative tops and panels; (3) riveted assembly as a durable alternative to solder in heat-prone lanterns; (4) an oxidation/aging process to achieve a 10–15 year patina finish; (5) final assembly including glass hurricane globe and electrical components; and (6) on-site exterior installation on a traditional New Orleans shotgun house, including upgrading to a proper junction box behind siding with weatherproof detailing and wiring that uses a licensed electrician. The video emphasizes craft technique, weatherproofing, and color choices (2700 K) to echo the historic gas-lit look.

video-electrical-upgrades-d3huy435l28-yo.summary: This This Old House segment documents a residential outdoor Level 2 EV charger installation at a house with no garage, positioned on the exterior wall at the far side of the driveway. The crew explains driving levels of charging (Level 1 through Level 3) and selects Level 2 for overnight charging, noting 8 hours can restore ~150–200 miles. They trench and trench-fill a conduit from under the driveway up to the house, pull wires through, install end fittings, glue and seat the conduit, and then make the three power connections inside the charger. The installation is described as weatherproof, outdoor-rated, and approved after consulting a local electrical inspector to ensure compliance with local and national codes. The video emphasizes practical placement to minimize cord length, outdoor equipment suitability, and considerations for future EV readiness.

video-electrical-upgrades-e4qtyatcmr0-yo.title: Task Lighting Upgrade in a Small Kitchen: Recessed Downlights and Under-Cabinet Fluorescents
video-electrical-upgrades-e4qtyatcmr0-yo.summary: This Old House demonstrates a kitchen lighting retrofit aimed at improving task illumination in a small space. The hosts replace two dim, nearby ceiling fixtures with two recessed LED/fluorescent-ready downlights (referred to as R40 blimps) to bring light down to the counter, and add complementary under-cabinet and above-cabinet fluorescent lighting (Thin Line) to brighten work surfaces and shelves. The project covers planning around existing sprinklers and ceiling obstructions, routing power from a single switch, creating ceiling penetrations, mounting fixtures with clips, hiding cords through cabinet fronts and crown molding, and testing the system for a brighter, more usable kitchen workspace.

video-electrical-upgrades-flyqyngjm7o-yo.title: Installing Wall Sconces in an Older Home: Wiring, Box Reuse, and Fireplace Mounting
video-electrical-upgrades-flyqyngjm7o-yo.summary: This This Old House episode follows Kevin and Heath as they troubleshoot and upgrade historical lighting around a living-room fireplace. They evaluate existing, nonfunctional wall switches, locate old plaster sconce boxes behind the fireplace, and determine that new wiring and larger boxes are required for proper, code-compliant sconces. The crew runs wire from the basement to a new wall location, uses a low-profile drilling trick to locate wall cavities, and pulls wires to the new sconces. They relocate a wall switch to a more logical position in the room, install the sconces, and patch the surrounding plaster. Throughout, they reference finding old wall contents (including a 1955 newspaper) as evidence of the wall’s history, and emphasize careful measurement from the mantel to ensure even, aesthetically pleasing sconce heights. The episode emphasizes planning, safe electrical work in an older home, and finishing touches for a clean install.

video-electrical-upgrades-gxrjwwrtkui-yo.title: Wiring a Portable Generator to a Home: Transfer Switch, Interlock, and Safety
video-electrical-upgrades-gxrjwwrtkui-yo.summary: This video demonstrates practical approaches to powering a home with a portable generator. It covers essential safety guidance for outdoor operation to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning, methods to feed a home from a generator using a power inlet box and backfed wiring, and two main approaches for safe electrical integration: a transfer switch that selects critical circuits and an interlock that isolates the generator from street power. The host emphasizes prioritizing critical loads (furnace, refrigerator, heating) and performing a controlled restoration by turning on loads one by one to avoid overloading the generator. It also cautions against running high-draw appliances (oven, dryer, central air) during a outage and notes that a generator has limited capacity relative to a whole-house load.

video-electrical-upgrades-hehwe7m1v4a-yo.title: Mount Outdoor TV with a Purpose-Built Enclosure: Wall mounting a 65-inch TV on an exterior deck
video-electrical-upgrades-hehwe7m1v4a-yo.summary: This Old House presents a practical indoor-to-outdoor TV upgrade by mounting a TV behind a purpose-built outdoor enclosure on an exterior wall of a shaded deck. The host team weighs sun exposure, selects a wall suitable for mounting, and sizes for a 65-inch screen. They replace an indoor TV setup with an enclosure that includes cooling fans, thermostats, and optional humidity/heat controls, and they implement a behind-the-TV receptacle with weatherproof, tamper-resistant hardware fed from a dedicated outdoor-rated circuit protected by an AFCI/GFCI breaker. The process covers spacing the TV on foam blocks inside the enclosure, aligning and bolting the enclosure to wall studs, routing and sealing power cords, and sealing mounting interfaces with silicone to maintain a watertight install. The project concludes with wiring, a final power test, and a demonstration that the TV returns a live signal on the new outdoor setup.

video-electrical-upgrades-i98j5-dipei-yo.title: Electrical Service Upgrade for a Two-Unit Home: From 200A to 400A with AFCI and Surge Protection
video-electrical-upgrades-i98j5-dipei-yo.summary: This Old House documents a two-unit home undergoing an electrical service upgrade tied to a broader renovation that includes new HVAC, appliances, and updated siding. The episode centers on determining electrical load and upgrading from a 200-amp service to a 400-amp service, driven by increased demand from two units and new equipment. It explains the path of utility power (the overhead triplex and point of attachment), the upgrade to a larger meter can, and the shift to two meters and two service panels to serve each unit. Interior wiring updates are noted (BX to NM wiring) along with modern code protections, including arc-fault circuit interrupters and surge protection installed at the panels. The video combines architectural context with practical electrical upgrading steps, emphasizing who is responsible for overhead infrastructure and how new protections help safeguard the home’s circuits and appliances.

video-electrical-upgrades-jjx5b8txc7e-yo.title: Diagnosing a High Electric Bill with Home Energy Monitoring (This Old House)
video-electrical-upgrades-jjx5b8txc7e-yo.summary: This This Old House episode follows a multi-tenant house facing a winter spike in electric bills. The team inventories the building’s electric loads, reviews the service and meter configuration, and uses analog meters to gauge real-time usage. They install a home energy monitoring system with current transformers (CTS) to isolate and track power draw across circuits, then perform controlled load-off tests to verify impact. After a two-month follow-up, they correlate real-time data with the utility bill to identify three major energy culprits—the mini-split heat pump, the well pump, and the electric water heater—and discuss practical savings (e.g., a hybrid heat-pump water heater) and the potential role of solar. The episode demonstrates a data-driven approach to diagnosing and reducing electricity costs in a multifamily home.

The process covers selecting fixtures (fluorescent T5), weighing LED alternatives, routing wiring from an attic power source through a top-plate drill, wiring the fixture to a master switch box, and employing a low-voltage transformer switch to provide flexible placement without a traditional electrical box. The demonstration includes basic wiring steps (hot to hot, neutral to neutral, ground to ground), mounting in a plastic box, and testing the final result with power restored.

video-electrical-upgrades-jyycb8tcyoc-yo.title: Drilling Holes for Electrical Wiring in Studs: Tools, Clearances, and Wire-Pulling Techniques
video-electrical-upgrades-jyycb8tcyoc-yo.summary: This Old House's Tool Lab video explains practical methods for boring holes in wood studs to run electrical wiring. It compares auger bits with self-feeding tops, spade bits, and a suite of accessories (extensions, right-angle adapters, flexible bits) to reach tight corners. The presenter emphasizes code-driven clearance from stud edges (minimum 1-1/4 inches) and suggests a center-spotting approach by stepping bit sizes to avoid precise centering on every stud. The workflow covers drilling demonstrations, corner access strategies, and wire-pulling techniques that keep wires at a consistent height, bend wires within the wall bay to form curves, and manage offsets with pre-fitting or “fish” methods. The video also notes protective measures like nail plates when clearance cannot be met and advises checking local codes for multiple cables.

video-electrical-upgrades-mqvvtna-9oa-yo.title: Undercabinet LED Tape Lighting with 24V Driver and Aluminum Channel Diffuser

An aluminum channel is mounted under the cabinets to keep the strip straight and to host a diffuser lens for even light. When a length is short, they add a 12-inch segment and snap in the diffuser. The result is a warm, bright countertop area suitable for kitchen tasks, with a sleek, concealed finish.

video-electrical-upgrades-ot-092vasxu-yo.title: Track Lighting Installation: Two-Circuit Track with App-Controlled Heads

It also shows dimming the heads and explains how the two circuits can be controlled either by a separate switch or via a mobile app, with the later segment highlighting Bluetooth-enabled fixtures that enable lighting control and music playback from a phone. Throughout, the steps emphasize practical wiring, mounting hardware, and the interaction between physical controls and app-based features.

video-electrical-upgrades-p0ta45tefqe-yo.title: Repairing a Three-Way Light Switch: Wiring, Testing, and Troubleshooting
video-electrical-upgrades-p0ta45tefqe-yo.summary: An Ask This Old House segment demonstrates diagnosing and repairing a miswired three-way light switch that controls a chandelier from two switches. The hosts cover the anatomy of single-pole versus three-way switches, show how to identify traveler wires and the common wire using a continuity tester and a lamp accessory, and guide the viewer through safely turning off power, labeling conductors, wiring the three-way correctly (traveler wires to the traveler screws and the common wire to the common terminal), and testing the setup to ensure both switches control the fixture as intended. A wiring diagram is used to illustrate how a typical three-way circuit functions, helping homeowners understand why the miswiring prevented operation.

video-electrical-upgrades-rngcwfg7ohm-yo.title: Convert a Recessed Light to a Pendant with Retrofit Socket Kit
video-electrical-upgrades-rngcwfg7ohm-yo.summary: This This Old House segment demonstrates converting a recessed light into a pendant using a retrofit socket kit. The host explains why simply removing the old fixture box is impractical due to the larger ceiling hole and hidden above-ceiling hardware, then introduces a socket adapter that plugs into the existing lamp base to power the new pendant. The kit uses a hollow mounting rod and bracket to suspend the pendant from the recessed housing, with a mounting plate attached to the rod and finished with medallions to conceal the opening. The process includes safety steps (power off, remove trims), wiring (black to black, white to white, green to ground), removing the old fixture bar, and installing an LED bulb for energy efficiency. The segment ends with powering the circuit back on and visually assessing the pendant lighting effect.

video-electrical-upgrades-unwes7h98ws-yo.title: Smart Outdoor Lighting Upgrade: Driveway, Garage, and Exterior Illumination
video-electrical-upgrades-unwes7h98ws-yo.summary: This Old House’s Ask This Old House episode guides a homeowner through upgrading to smart outdoor lighting for a dark driveway approach, a dim top-of-stairs light, and a bright yet neighbor-conscious exterior. The hosts compare LED tape options (low-voltage 24 V) and 120 V strips, propose landscape wall lights as a scalable, low-glare solution, and emphasize practical considerations such as layout spacing (roughly every six feet), wire concealment beneath trim, and weatherproofing. The plan evolves to include a transformer for low-voltage lighting, a trim-down on glare by choosing wall-pack-style fixtures for the garage, and the integration of smart controls (a basement-based neutral-enabled smart switch and an exterior smart plug) for centralized control and scenes. The demonstration culminates with a completed layout and a successful test scene, showcasing a brighter, controllable exterior lighting system without excessive glare or neighbor disruption.

video-electrical-upgrades-wlmivbm-zj4-yo.title: Outdoor Movie Night Tech Essentials: Projector, Power, and Sound
video-electrical-upgrades-wlmivbm-zj4-yo.summary: This This Old House segment inventories practical tech for outdoor movie nights, focusing on a projector-based setup, wireless connectivity, portable power, and weather-rated audio hardware. Viewers see how an outdoor-friendly projector can replace a wall-mounted TV, how Bluetooth and Wi‑Fi enable content and smart-home integration, and how a rollable solar-rechargeable battery bank powers the setup with real-world specs (about 1,000 Wh capacity and roughly 90 W load). The discussion covers solar charging options, USB/12V/120V outputs, and a portable speaker option versus permanent outdoor speakers, including IP ratings and UV protection as critical outdoor considerations. The segment also demonstrates smart outdoor plugs for scheduling and weatherproof outlets to manage the movie-night electronics. Collectively, it presents a practical blueprint for coordinating display, audio, power, and weather resistance in an outdoor entertainment environment.

video-electrical-upgrades-y4kk3inpnhy-yo.title: Updating an Old Electrical System: From BX to NM in a Historic Home
video-electrical-upgrades-y4kk3inpnhy-yo.summary: This This Old House episode documents a retrofit of an older home’s electrical system. The hosts discover armored BX cable throughout the house and place the work in historical context, noting that the structure likely dates from the late 19th to early 20th century and that knob-and-tube wiring would have been expected in some periods but is not present. They explain key wiring generations: knob-and-tube (single-conductor, routed through studs with knobs and tubes), BX/armored cable (two conductors in one jacket with external protection), and modern NM cable (nonmetallic sheathed, two conductors plus ground). The discussion highlights practical differences, including ease of installation, pull-through capability, and color-coding (yellow jacket indicating 20-amp NM).
